It's a little more complicated than that, but that's what it comes down to. They take it one way, the other, or both. Your income is not taxed up to a certain point that depends on the number of dependents/exemptions you have (for a single adult, it's usually about $10,000). Some of that is not taxed at all, but most is taxed at 10%. After that, it's taxed at a bracketed scale, along the lines of 10,000-40,000 is taxed at 12%, 40k-85k at 15%, etc, through 520k and above taxed at 37% (i.e. the portion of your income that falls in that range is taxed at that rate, and only the portion above and in the next tax bracket is taxed at the next higher rate - this stuff about giving away income so you don't fall in a higher tax bracket makes no sense there).

So yeah, I might have been a bit off for the exact percentage, but my family's effective tax rate percentage is in the high 20s.

Depending on how you structure and manage your income, you might have it withheld as part of your pay schedule (that is, your employer uses information you provide about your dependents and deduction to calculate an amount to note on your pay record and send directly to the IRS - this is how it is done for most people), or you might have none deducted and have to estimate and make quarterly payments then make a final calculation and pay the balance between 1 jan and 15 april of the next year. Generally, anyone may choose either withholding or self-payment, though with either way the individual taxpayer is expected to pay any additional amount they actually owe if the estimate and prepayments were not sufficient to cover the final calculation of what they owe (or they should expect a refund of what they paid in excess of what they owed if the final calculation for the year was in their favor).
